Issued at 305 AM EST Fri Nov 6 2026

Early Friday morning, a cold front was draped from roughly St. 
Louis, Missouri to Muncie, Indiana. With and behind the front, low 
clouds and patchy drizzle have been observed, along with an uptick 
in winds which have sporadically gusted over 20 mph from the north-
northwest.

*** CLOUDY WITH PATCHY DRIZZLE TODAY ***

The aforementioned front and its attendant gloomy weather will 
arrive early to mid morning from northwest to southeast, and linger 
into the evening across much of the area. This will keep daytime 
temperatures on the cool side; forecast highs range from the low 60s 
across the Lake Cumberland Region to the mid 50s north of I-64. Time 
heights suggest saturation is mainly above 1,000 ft which lowers 
confidence in any drizzle particularly during the afternoon, but 
certainly can't rule it out as the RAP shows some transient 
visibility reductions along with modest negative omega (rising 
motion) along the front.

*** FROST AND FREEZE THIS WEEKEND ***

Some uncertainty remains in when the back edge of the stratus will 
shift out of the local area, but the latest REFS probabilities for 
cloud cover drop quickly from north to south between 8pm and 2am 
EST. This will foster efficient radiational cooling tonight, 
particularly near and west of the I-65 corridor where winds should 
go calm as surface high pressure settles in. As a result, I elected 
not to deviate from NBM's forecast temperatures which are running on 
the low end of model guidance and depict Saturday morning lows 
anywhere from the upper 30s in the heart of the Louisville Metro to 
mid 30s over southern Kentucky to around 30 in rural, low-lying 
areas (1) west of I-65 and (2) in the northern Bluegrass. Given the 
uncertainty on when skies clear and winds go slack, didn't feel 
confident enough to issue a Freeze Warning for any part of our area 
for tonight, though again freezing temperatures are a distinct 
possibility in rural valleys. It's noteworthy that trying to 
quantify the probability is a bit tricky in this case, since 
virtually zero REFS members have temperatures < 33, while NBM's 
calibrated guidance suggests chances are as high as 70-80+% in 
spots; given REFS has been a few degrees too warm on overnight lows 
recently, we're going to lean towards NBM, but still think it's 
chances might be at least slightly overdone. Nonetheless, confidence 
is high (>80%) in frost nearly everywhere (save perhaps downtown 
Louisville, where the urban heat island may keep temps in the upper 
30s); accordingly, we've issued a Frost Advisory, which is in effect 
from midnight to 9am EST tomorrow morning.

Confidence in a true freeze is higher (60-80%) tomorrow night into 
Sunday morning, as night-long clear skies and calm winds cause 
temperatures to sink like a rock. However, we elected to hold off on 
a Freeze Watch for now for simplicity sake.

Conditions will remain seasonably cool through the weekend, but 
temperatures should take a turn for the warmer early next work week 
as upper level ridging returns to yield highs solidly in the 60s 
Monday through Wednesday. Given the dry airmass, chilly, crisp 
mornings will continue with patchy frost possible each day, but 
after the widespread freeze Saturday night (and possibly again 
Sunday night over the Bluegrass) we don't think the corresponding 
headlines will be required again until spring.

Looking at EOF patterns for 500mb height in the LREF, uncertainty is 
high primarily in the east-west "zonal" position of a broad upper 
level trough expected to dive southeast out of Canada during the 
latter portion of the week. Two general scenarios have emerged from 
cluster analysis: outcome (a), favored by ~60% of guidance, would 
bring a few showers to the area Thursday-Friday followed by a 
cooldown next weekend; outcome (b) (40% chance) would keep us dry 
and mild, as the cooler air remains locked up across the Great Lakes 
and New England.
